**Tier 5** — results — pinned to dataset + policy + engine version · owned by `engine` · `public.simulation_jobs`

**One row is** One queued run of the RETIRED batch pipeline: a project, the legacy disruption profiles it applied, a priority, a status and progress, and a pointer to the `simulation_results` row it produced. It was the queue between `simulation-runner` and `external-simulation-processor` / the Render-hosted `ml-service`. Tier 5 — run bookkeeping for a result, input to nothing. DORMANT IN THE REPOSITORY: no code in `src/`, `supabase/functions/`, `sim-worker/` or `scsim/` reads or writes it. The current product's run queue is `simulation_runs`, driven by `sim-command` and the Fly worker, and it never touches this table.

A RETIRED PIPELINE'S QUEUE, LEFT IN PLACE ON PURPOSE by the 2026-07-02 commit that removed the legacy batch stack ("left in place, inert, for a later cleanup migration"). A drop needs a production row count first, which no §15 run has taken, and D168's live legacy functions are a reason to take one. THE SHADOWED DEFINITION IS RESOLVED, AND THE ARTIFACT ALREADY HAD THE ANSWER. `20250913085427` created this table with no `job_id`; `20250914113723` re-declared it with `job_id TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL`, `plant_name`, `current_stage` and three CHECKs (`valid_status`, `valid_job_type`, `valid_priority`). The re-declaration never took effect, by three independent lines of evidence. (1) Its `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` was a no-op against the existing table, and its later `CREATE INDEX … (job_id)` names a column that table did not have, so PostgreSQL raised 42703 and the whole file rolled back — §4 D97, which taught the introspector to record a rejected statement as an abort; `build/schema.introspected.json` lists `20250914113723` under `aborted_migrations` for that reason, so the columns above come from `20250913085427` alone. (2) Production agrees: §4 D30's trigger probe (§15 run `35064364537`) found all four of `20250913085427`'s triggers and NONE of `20250914113723`'s, so the later file never ran to its end there. (3) Its author knew: `20250914113757`, 34 seconds later, is titled "Fix existing simulation_jobs table structure" and ADDs `job_id TEXT` (nullable), backfills it with `id::text`, adds `simulation_jobs_job_id_key UNIQUE (job_id)` and ADDs `current_stage` — the shape recorded here. So: `job_id` is NULLABLE text with a unique constraint, `plant_name` was never a column, and the `job_type`/`priority` CHECKs do not exist (the legacy runner wrote `job_type` values 'baseline' and 'scenarios', which `valid_job_type` would have refused — consistent with it never landing). The one residual risk is a fresh database replayed from empty, where `20250914113723` has nothing to collide with and would run — D30's closing sentence, unchanged.

Two policies through the project's organization (`org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization)`): SELECT for any member of that organization, ALL for the project's modeler or an organization admin — recreated in that form by WP 2.1's `20260915000004`, which is why the duplicate-policy question of §4 D30 no longer leaves the end state in doubt. Neither policy is predicate-less, so `write: null` agrees with `governanceEnforcement.test.ts`, and no user-facing write path exists in the repository. Two BEFORE triggers still fire on any write (`simulation_jobs_defaults`, `simulation_job_timing_trigger`); the AFTER trigger that once posted every new job to `external-simulation-processor` was dropped on 2025-09-19, so the database no longer calls out on a write. Deleting a project removes its jobs through the inline `REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE`. NOT IN PRODUCTION'S CASE: §4 D168 found the legacy functions that wrote this queue (`simulation-runner`, `external-simulation-processor`, `simulation-status`, `delete-simulation-job`) still LIVE in production with no source here. "Dormant" is true of the repository; whether those endpoints are still called is D168's production question (WP 7.1). NOT AUDITED: tier 5, and `audit-actor` covers tiers 2–4.
